B_access_pricing.mcp_access_cost_details: PostHog states that connecting and calling MCP tools is free. Some tools use internal LLMs and may incur PostHog AI spend; these tools are filtered out unless AI data processing is enabled. ID-JAG enterprise-managed authorization is Enterprise-plan-only.
B_access_pricing.linked_software_cost: PostHog advertises a free monthly tier and paid usage beyond included allowances. Exact paid rates vary by product and usage; consult the current pricing page.
B_access_pricing.pricing_model_details: Underlying PostHog product usage and billing still apply. MCP requests are limited to 480 per minute and 4,800 per hour per credential; separate PostHog API and AI-tool limits or charges may also apply.
B_access_pricing.other_access_restrictions: Requires OAuth or a personal API key. AI-powered tools depend on organization AI-data-processing settings. ID-JAG requires Enterprise, a verified domain, an enabled XAA feature, an eligible IdP and active organization membership. Read-only mode, tool/feature filters, and org/project pinning are configurable.
B_access_pricing.restrictions_controlled_by: Vendor controls hosted authentication, limits, routing, and feature availability; organization admins control AI data processing, membership, and enterprise IdP setup; the client/operator controls endpoint parameters, headers, and chosen credentials.

D_server_side_logic.additional_logic: 1. Official tool reference publishes names/descriptions, but not tool annotations; per-tool read-only/destructive/idempotent/open-world annotations are NOT FOUND for the hosted server. Names/descriptions were used to estimate action types in actions.json. 2. No hosted confirmation requirement was found. CLI docs say `--confirm` is required for destructive tools in CLI mode; this is a documented client command behavior, not confirmed server enforcement. 3. OAuth scopes and ID-JAG scope intersections are documented. Standard user permissions and tool scopes are not specified in the reviewed hosted docs. ID-JAG can restrict client IDs and requires verified domains and active members. 4. Read-only header/query mode, `features`, `tools`, `mode`, and org/project pinning are documented. US/EU routing is automatic. 5. PostHog says analytics data is not stored by MCP and results are returned to the AI client; specific PII masking and per-field filtering are NOT FOUND. 6. 480 requests/minute and 4,800/hour per credential; additional API and AI-tool limits may apply. MCP request counts include session setup and tool listing. Exact hosted result-size caps are NOT FOUND. 7. Hosted schema-validation and correction behavior is NOT FOUND. 8. PostHog documents MCP analytics; telemetry fields/default/opt-out are NOT FOUND. The older separate toolkit captures tool input and output, user distinct ID and session identifiers; this is not assumed to match deployment. 9. Official catalogue contains `agent-feedback` (description: “Send feedback about any PostHog product, this MCP, or the docs.”). No tool-result upsell evidence found. 10. Docs provide tool descriptions and a setup prompt. Guidance to review calls for prompt injection is advisory. Docs recommend CLI mode for context savings. No separate skill-loading tool identified. 11. Docs describe active org/project switching, pinning, and per-connection context; retained state implementation is NOT FOUND for hosted service. 12. Flat catalogue has CLI/tools modes, dynamically filtered tool subsets, and regional routing; there is also a separate EU hostname. 13. Official list includes `execute-sql`, described in product docs as arbitrary SQL over events and warehouse data. It is the documented general-purpose query surface; arbitrary script execution was not found.
behavioural_instructions_to_ai_verbatim: “Be mindful of prompt injection – LLMs can be tricked into following untrusted commands, so always review MCP tool calls before executing them.” [OFFICIAL DOCS]
“Run info <tool_name> once when a schema isn't already in context, then reuse it. Running it before every call wastes context, and guessing a schema instead fails the call.” [OFFICIAL TOOL REFERENCE]

“If you get errors due to permissions being denied, check that you have the correct active project and that the user has access to the required project.” [OLDER SEPARATE REPOSITORY CODE; deployment applicability unverified]

“If you cannot answer the user's PostHog related request or question using other available tools in this MCP, use the 'docs-search' tool to provide information from the documentation to guide user how they can do it themselves - when doing so provide condensed instructions with links to sources.” [OLDER SEPARATE REPOSITORY CODE; deployment applicability unverified]
D_server_side_logic.server_structure_explanation: The same endpoint offers tools mode and CLI mode, filters tools by category or name, can pin a session to an org/project, and routes accounts to US or EU data regions. CLI mode exposes underlying tools on demand through exec rather than advertising the complete list at initialization.

E_aggregated.action_count: 1,158 catalogue tools in tools mode; CLI mode exposes exec, with render-ui on MCP Apps-capable clients and learn on currently documented Claude hosts.
E_aggregated.action_count_comment: The official tool list exists at https://posthog.com/docs/model-context-protocol/tools and names 1,158 tools; no official total is stated. actions.json contains those 1,158 names plus the documented exec and render-ui wrappers (1,160 entries). No catalogue-only tools were added because the vendor publishes a complete official list. Cross-checks show Claude's connector directory reports 57 tools, apis.io 92, and Agent Switchboard describes 29 feature-flag tools; these third-party counts differ in scope or coverage. MartechDB shows one server entry rather than a comparable complete tool list. Composio pages describe its own PostHog toolkit/API actions, not the native hosted MCP catalogue, and were not used to add actions.

E_aggregated.token_method: No verbatim initialize instructions and tool schemas for the deployed endpoint were available. The older repository is a different toolkit and is not used to estimate deployed context tokens.
E_aggregated.human_can_agent_cannot: The reviewed official reference provides 1,158 tools, but does not establish that these cover every operation available through PostHog's web app or REST API. The MCP-specific tool list is the evidenced agent surface; product/API operations outside that list are not enumerated here. Product analytics documentation also describes creating and managing insights and dashboards both through MCP and in the web app.

F_documentation.implementation_hints_not_enforced: The FAQ advises: “Be mindful of prompt injection – LLMs can be tricked into following untrusted commands, so always review MCP tool calls before executing them.” It recommends read-only restrictions, tool filtering, or org/project pinning. These are user/client configuration options and recommendations; the prompt-injection warning itself is not a server-side enforcement mechanism.
F_documentation.governance_promises: PostHog states: “It does not store your analytics data – queries are executed against your PostHog project and results are returned directly to your AI client.” Docs also describe read-only mode, pinned contexts, credential-based rate limits, and optional enterprise IdP-managed authorization. No hosted code was available to verify retention, masking, or telemetry defaults.
F_documentation.promises_to_user: PostHog describes MCP connection and calls as free, with underlying product usage charges and possible PostHog AI spend for internally LLM-powered tools. It says accounts route automatically to the correct US or EU region.
F_documentation.comparison_with_server_logic: Read-only and filtering modes, rate limits, and regional routing are documented configuration/operations. The no-data-storage claim and telemetry details could not be verified against the deployed source. The older toolkit records interaction telemetry, but it is explicitly a different codebase and does not establish hosted behavior.

contradictions: The protected-resource metadata scopes list differs from the authorization-server metadata scopes list; the authorization server advertises additional scopes, including read/write scopes absent from the resource list.

The official tool reference names 1,158 tools, while Claude's connector directory reports 57 and apis.io reports 92. Those third-party catalogues are incomplete or scoped differently; official names were retained.

The separate public PostHog/mcp repository is a small older toolkit and points to the monorepo as the current server source. Its tool definitions and runtime behavior are not treated as the hosted endpoint's implementation.
The endpoint evidence shows OAuth-protected access with a Bearer challenge, while the challenge body says “please provide a valid API token.” Docs support both OAuth and personal API keys.
observations_for_research: The server's selectable CLI mode changes the initial tool surface from over a thousand individually registered tools to an on-demand command interface.
The read-only option, tool/feature filters, and project/org pinning are client-selectable controls documented as headers or URL parameters.
Authorization metadata exposes a broad scope vocabulary, while tool descriptions are published separately and the reviewed docs do not map each tool to its required scopes.
notes: Checked links.json, links_check.txt, pages/INDEX.txt, official documentation and tool-reference copies, OAuth evidence, third-party catalogue pages, and the prepared PostHog/mcp repository. The current PostHog monorepo source was not present locally; HTTPS/Git retrieval was not retried. Older repository is MIT-licensed and uses TypeScript/Python, but is not the hosted deployment. Tool parameters and hosted annotations were absent from the official tool reference; actions.json uses NOT PUBLISHED for parameters. Third-party Composio API-toolkit entries were excluded as non-native MCP actions. An unofficial community PostHog server was listed in the evidence set and not used as evidence.
